If Babylon is Jerusalem, why is the harlot riding the beast, which looks like Rome?
On this reading, riding the beast shows alliance, not identity. Jerusalem's leaders partnered with Rome against Jesus and his followers.

The beast has seven heads, which John links with seven hills (Revelation 17:9). Many see Rome there. The fulfilled reading agrees that the beast is Rome. But the woman is distinct from the beast she rides. So she is not Rome. She is a city in league with Rome. The Gospels show such an alliance. The chief priests brought Jesus to Pilate because they could not legally execute him (John 18:28-32). They cried, 'We have no king but Caesar' (John 19:15). In Thessalonica opponents accused Paul's friends of acting against Caesar's decrees (Acts 17:7). In the end the beast and ten horns turn on the harlot and burn her (Revelation 17:16), as Rome burned Jerusalem in AD 70.
John 19:12-15: 'If you release this man, you are not Caesar's friend.'
Josephus, Jewish War 6.4.5-7: the temple burned in August AD 70; the city followed in September.
Revelation 17:16: the ten horns hate the harlot and burn her with fire.

Those who see Rome reply that the woman is 'the great city that rules over the kings of the earth' (Revelation 17:18). That fits Rome far better than Jerusalem. They read 17:16 as Rome destroyed from within, or as a world system turning on itself. Futurists see a future religious system destroyed by the Antichrist's empire.
Can an Old Testament name like Sodom, Egypt or Babylon be used for a different city?
Yes. Scripture often gives a city a symbolic name to show its character. Revelation itself calls the city where Jesus was crucified 'Sodom and Egypt'.

On this reading, these names are a kind of prophetic shorthand. Revelation 11:8 says the great city is called 'spiritually' (or 'mystically') Sodom and Egypt, 'where also their Lord was crucified'. That is clearly Jerusalem. Isaiah called Judah's rulers 'rulers of Sodom' (Isaiah 1:10). He said they paraded their sin like Sodom (3:9). Ezekiel said Jerusalem's harlotry began in Egypt (Ezekiel 23:3, 8, 19). Revelation also calls a false teacher at Thyatira 'Jezebel' (Revelation 2:20). So 'Babylon' need not mean the city on the Euphrates. It names a city that acts like Babylon: proud, rich, idolatrous and a persecutor of God's people. The Old Testament Babylon prophecies themselves are fulfilled.
Revelation 11:8: Sodom and Egypt, 'where their Lord was crucified'.
Isaiah 1:9-10: 'rulers of Sodom... people of Gomorrah' addresses Jerusalem.
Revelation 2:20: 'that woman Jezebel' at Thyatira, a symbolic name.

Most interpreters agree that 'Babylon' in Revelation is symbolic. They disagree about the target. Many early Christians and modern scholars apply it to Rome, as in 1 Peter 5:13. Reformation writers often applied it to the papacy. Some futurists hold that Revelation 18 requires a literal rebuilt city.
Do Bible scholars agree that Gog, 'prince of Rosh,' is the leader of Russia?
No. Many leading scholars, including evangelicals, reject the link. It rests on similar sounds, not on Hebrew grammar or ancient geography.

Some popular books say 'Bible scholars agree' that Gog of Ezekiel 38-39 is Russia's leader. They do not. The theory works like this. The Hebrew word rosh is taken as a nation's name. It sounds like 'Russia'. Meshech sounds like 'Moscow'. Tubal sounds like 'Tobolsk', a Siberian city. The fulfilled reading, with many evangelical scholars, rejects this. The historian Edwin Yamauchi wrote that rosh can have nothing to do with modern Russia. He added that informed studies call the Moscow and Tobolsk links untenable. Even some dispensational scholars now agree. Sound-alike word games are not a sound way to read any text. We must ask what the words meant to Ezekiel and his first hearers.
Moscow is first mentioned in 1147 AD. Tobolsk was founded in 1587 AD.
Edwin Yamauchi, 'Foes from the Northern Frontier' (1982), studies the steppe peoples and rejects the Russia link.

Many popular futurists still hold the Russia view. Some scholars defend 'Rosh' as a proper name, citing the Greek Septuagint ('Rhos') and possible ancient place names such as Rashu. They usually do not equate it with modern Russia by sound alone. Some say it is a people of the far north, and Russia now holds that territory.
What does the Hebrew word rosh mean in Ezekiel 38:2?
Rosh normally means 'head' or 'chief'. Many translations read 'chief prince of Meshech and Tubal'. 'Russia' comes from 'Rus', a medieval name.

The word rosh appears hundreds of times in the Hebrew Bible. It means 'head', 'top', 'first' or 'chief'. The high priest is the kohen ha-rosh, the chief priest (2 Kings 25:18). In Ezekiel 38:2 the phrase can be read as 'Gog... the chief prince of Meshech and Tubal'. The King James Version, the ESV and the NIV read it this way. The name 'Russia' comes from the Rus, Scandinavian traders who settled around Kiev in the 9th century AD. That is fifteen centuries after Ezekiel. The fulfilled reading also notes that Rosh never appears as a people's name anywhere else in the Old Testament. The 19th-century scholar Hengstenberg said the Russians had been placed among God's enemies unjustly.
2 Kings 25:18: 'Seraiah the chief priest' uses rosh for 'chief'.
The Russian Primary Chronicle dates the coming of the Rus leader Rurik to about AD 862.
King James Version, Ezekiel 38:2: 'the chief prince of Meshech and Tubal'.

Some scholars argue that the Hebrew accents and grammar favour a place name: 'prince of Rosh, Meshech and Tubal'. The Greek Septuagint, NASB and NKJV read it so. They link it to ancient peoples called Rashu or Rosh. But most do not say that sound alone proves Russia.
Where were Meshech and Tubal in Ezekiel's day?
In Anatolia, modern Turkey. Assyrian records name them Mushku and Tabal. They were not in Russia.

On this reading, ancient records settle the question. Assyrian inscriptions from the 12th to 7th centuries BC name Mushku and Tabal. They were peoples of central and eastern Anatolia, in today's Turkey. Mushku is linked with the Phrygians of King Midas (Assyrian 'Mita'), about 700 BC. In the Bible, Meshech and Tubal are sons of Japheth (Genesis 10:2). Ezekiel names them as traders with Tyre in slaves and bronze (Ezekiel 27:13). He also names them among the fallen nations in the grave (32:26). So these are real peoples Ezekiel's hearers knew. Herodotus mentions the Moschoi and Tibarenoi near the Black Sea (Histories 3.94; 7.78). They are not modern cities with similar sounds.
Assyrian annals of Sargon II (about 715 BC) mention Mita of Mushku.
Herodotus 7.78: the Moschoi and Tibarenoi served in Xerxes' army in 480 BC.
Ezekiel 27:13: Javan, Tubal and Meshech traded slaves and bronze with Tyre.

Many futurist scholars now accept that Meshech and Tubal were in Anatolia. They say Ezekiel names ancient peoples whose lands are today occupied by Turkey and nearby states. These nations could join a future coalition led from the far north. Some older writers still cite Moscow and Tobolsk.
Where did the idea that Rosh means Russia come from?
It grew in the 19th century. The lexicographer Wilhelm Gesenius suggested it, John Cumming popularized it in 1864, and the Scofield Reference Bible spread it widely in 1909.

The Rosh-Russia link is fairly recent. Some Byzantine writers in the 10th century linked the Rus with Ezekiel's 'Rhos' after Rus raids on Constantinople. But the modern form grew in the 1800s. The German scholar Wilhelm Gesenius suggested in his Hebrew lexicon that Rosh might refer to the Russians. In 1864 the Scottish preacher John Cumming wrote that the 'king of the north' was the Russian ruler. He claimed nearly all expositors agreed. The Scofield Reference Bible (1909) said 'all agree' that Russia is meant. Later writers repeated this through the Cold War. The fulfilled reading notes that a claim of total agreement was never true. Many expositors, such as Hengstenberg, rejected it.
Scofield Reference Bible (1909), note on Ezekiel 38:2.
Crimean War (1853-1856): Britain fought Russia, and many British preachers read Russia into prophecy.
Hal Lindsey, 'The Late Great Planet Earth' (1970), quoted Cumming.

Futurist defenders reply that the identification is older than Gesenius in some sources. They also argue that a doctrine's history does not decide its truth. The question is whether the Hebrew supports 'Rosh' as a place. Some cite a 2nd-millennium BC Egyptian or Ugaritic name as evidence.
Doesn't 'the remote parts of the north' in Ezekiel 38 point to Russia?
Not necessarily. In the Bible 'north' is often the direction from which invaders came, not their homeland. Babylon, in the east, is called a foe 'from the north'.

Ezekiel says Gog will come from the remote parts of the north (Ezekiel 38:6, 15; 39:2). Russia does lie north of Israel. But the fulfilled reading points out how the Bible uses 'north'. Jeremiah warned of disaster from the north (Jeremiah 1:14; 4:6; 6:1, 22). That was Babylon, which lies to the east. Armies from Mesopotamia did not cross the Arabian desert. They followed the Fertile Crescent and entered Israel from the north. Zephaniah places Assyria in the north (Zephaniah 2:13). Isaiah says Cyrus of Persia came from the north as well (Isaiah 41:25). The Bible atlas writer Barry Beitzel notes that 'north' marks the direction of approach. The far north of Ezekiel's day was the region of the Black and Caspian seas.
Jeremiah 4:6: 'I am bringing evil from the north.' This came true when Babylon took Jerusalem in 586 BC.
Isaiah 41:25: one 'from the north' and 'from the rising of the sun' (Cyrus).
Psalms 48:2: Mount Zion is described as 'in the far north'. 'North' can carry symbolic meaning.

Futurists answer that 'remote parts' or 'uttermost north' means the farthest north, and Moscow lies almost directly north of Jerusalem. They argue this is stronger than the ordinary 'from the north'. Some scholars treat the 'north' as symbolic of chaos and hostile powers.
Do the nations listed with Gog (Persia, Cush, Put, Gomer, Togarmah) describe a modern coalition?
On this reading, they describe the known world of Ezekiel's day. If Rosh means Russia because of sound, why do the other names not sound like modern nations?

Some futurists give three reasons for a modern Russian-led attack. Some of Ezekiel's nations lived in lands now in Russia. The armies come from the far north. Many of the nations are today allies of Russia. The fulfilled reading answers that these are ancient names of ancient peoples. Persia, Cush (south of Egypt), Put (Libya), Gomer (the Cimmerians) and Beth-togarmah (eastern Anatolia) all existed in the Persian era. Political alliances change every few years. Ezekiel's list also points to the edges of the Persian Empire, which stretched 'from India to Cush' (Esther 1:1). Finally, if sound-alike names reveal modern nations, then Gomer and Put should also sound like modern countries. They do not.
Esther 1:1 and 8:9: 127 provinces from India to Cush.
Gomer: the Cimmerians (Assyrian 'Gimirrai') invaded Anatolia in the 7th century BC.
Soviet relations with Israel shifted: arms deals were offered by 1991 and full relations restored in October 1991.

Futurists reply that Ezekiel used the names of his day for the lands that modern nations occupy. Persia is Iran; Cush is Sudan; Put is Libya; Gomer and Togarmah are Turkey. They see current ties between Russia, Iran and Turkey as a striking match. Others read the list as symbolic of all nations from the earth's edges.
Is the Gog and Magog battle of Revelation 20 the same as Ezekiel 38-39?
On this reading, no. Revelation places its Gog and Magog after the thousand years, and the details differ. John uses the old name for a new event.

Many futurists place Ezekiel's battle in a future seven-year tribulation. But the fulfilled reading notes that Gog, Magog, Meshech and Tubal are never named in Revelation 4-19, where futurists place the tribulation. Revelation 20:7-9 names Gog and Magog only after the thousand years. The details also differ. In Ezekiel, Gog comes from the north with named nations. In Revelation, the nations come from the four corners of the earth. In Ezekiel, the dead are buried over seven months (39:12). In Revelation, fire comes down and consumes them (20:9). So John uses Ezekiel's name as a type, just as he uses Jezebel (2:20), Sodom and Egypt (11:8) and Babylon (14:8). Ezekiel's event is past. Revelation's is a new event.
Ezekiel 39:12: seven months to bury Gog's dead.
Revelation 20:9: fire comes from heaven and devours the attackers.
Revelation 20:8: 'the four corners of the earth', not only the far north.

Some amillennialists hold that Revelation 19:17-21, 20:7-10 and Ezekiel 38-39 all describe the same final battle at Christ's return. They note that Revelation 19:17-18 quotes Ezekiel 39:17-20. Some premillennialists see Ezekiel 38-39 fulfilled before or at the start of the millennium, and Revelation 20 as a separate later revolt.
Do 'the latter years' and 'the last days' in Ezekiel 38:8, 16 mean the end of the world?
Not necessarily. The Hebrew phrase means 'in the days to come'. Scripture uses it for events in Israel's history, such as the time of the judges and the exile.

The Hebrew phrase acharit ha-yamim literally means 'the after part of the days'. On this reading, it simply means 'in the future', since Hebrew had no single word for that idea. Moses warned that evil would come on Israel 'in the latter days' (Deuteronomy 31:29). Judges 2:20 shows Israel breaking the covenant soon after Joshua's death. Jeremiah said Judah would understand God's judgment 'in the latter days' (Jeremiah 30:24). He promised to restore Moab and Elam 'in the latter days' (48:47; 49:39). Modern versions often translate these 'in days to come'. Jacob also used the phrase for the future of his sons' tribes (Genesis 49:1). Nothing in the phrase itself requires thousands of years.
Genesis 49:1: Jacob tells what will befall his sons 'in the last days'.
Jeremiah 48:47 and 49:39: Moab and Elam restored 'in the latter days'. Many versions translate 'in days to come'.
Numbers 24:14: Balaam's oracle 'in the latter days', often linked to David's victories over Moab.

Futurists agree the phrase can mean 'the future'. But they say that in many prophetic texts it points to the messianic age or the end (Isaiah 2:2; Hosea 3:5; Daniel 10:14). In Ezekiel 38 it follows the promise of the Spirit and national restoration (Ezekiel 36-37). New Testament writers say the 'last days' began with Christ (Hebrews 1:2; Acts 2:17).
Doesn't Ezekiel 38:8 require Israel to be regathered from many nations, which only happened after 1948?
On this reading, no. Israel had already been scattered among many nations by Ezekiel's time. God promised to gather them after seventy years, and he did.

Futurists teach that Israel was scattered among the nations only after AD 70. So they place the regathering in modern times. The fulfilled reading answers from Ezekiel and Jeremiah. Ezekiel, writing in exile, says God scattered Israel among the nations (Ezekiel 12:15; 6:8-9). The northern tribes had been deported by Assyria in 722 BC. Judah went to Babylon and Egypt. Jeremiah promised that God would gather his people 'from all the nations' (Jeremiah 29:14). He gave the time: after seventy years in Babylon (29:10). Ezra and Nehemiah record that return, beginning in 538 BC. Ezekiel 37 promises a united people in the land. Ezekiel 38 then pictures them living securely in unwalled villages (38:11), as in the Persian period before Nehemiah rebuilt the walls.
Ezekiel 12:15: 'I scatter them among the nations.'
Jews lived across the Persian Empire. Esther 3:8 speaks of 'a certain people scattered abroad' in all provinces.
Ezekiel 38:11: 'unwalled villages... without walls, bars or gates.' Jerusalem's walls were rebuilt in 445 BC (Nehemiah 6:15).

Futurists reply that the return from Babylon was small and from few lands. They see Ezekiel 38:8, 12 and Isaiah 11:11 ('the second time') as requiring a worldwide return. They hold this began in the 19th and 20th centuries. They also say Israel has not yet 'dwelt securely', so the battle is still future.
Why does Ezekiel describe horses, swords, bows and wooden weapons if the battle is in our future?
On this reading, because the battle is ancient. Attempts to fit wooden weapons into modern warfare become strained.

Ezekiel describes horsemen (38:4, 15), shields, swords, bows, arrows, war clubs and spears (39:9). The weapons are burned as firewood for seven years (39:9-10). These point to a war in a pre-industrial age. Futurists who read the text literally must explain this. Some say armies will return to old weapons. One writer claimed the Russians had made a wooden rifle of compressed wood, harder than steel and lighter. No source was given. Compressed wood is heavy, and modern light weapons use plastics and composites. In 1940 Harry Rimmer guessed that new rays would make metal weapons useless. The fulfilled reading sees these as signs of a forced literalism. The plain reading is that Ezekiel described a battle with weapons of his own era.
Ezekiel 39:9-10: weapons used as fuel for seven years.
Harry Rimmer, 'The Coming War and the Rise of Russia' (1940), proposed wooden weapons for a future war.
Some writers read Ezekiel's 'horses' as engine 'horsepower'.

Some futurists say God may use ancient language for modern arms, or that wooden weapons will be literal after a global collapse. Others see the battle as apocalyptic and symbolic. Its weapons and seven years show total victory, and no literal timing is meant. Many amillennialists take this symbolic view.
If Ezekiel 38-39 is not a future war, when was it fulfilled?
One proposal places it in the days of Esther. Haman plotted to destroy and plunder the Jews across the Persian Empire. The plot backfired, and the Jews defeated their enemies.

This reading follows the order of Ezekiel. Ezekiel 34-37 promises a shepherd, a new heart and a revived people in the land. That fits the first return under Zerubbabel and Joshua the high priest (Ezra 3; Zechariah 3). Ezekiel 38-39 then describes enemies from all over the empire attacking a peaceful people. Ezekiel 40-48 describes a restored temple order in figurative terms. The writer James B. Jordan proposed that Gog's attack matches Haman's plot (Esther 3:8-15). Haman's decree let enemies attack the Jews in all 127 provinces, from India to Cush (Esther 8:9). Instead the Jews struck their enemies (9:5). God turned the plot back on its maker. The feast of Purim marks this victory (9:20-28).
Esther 9:16: 75,000 enemies killed in the provinces.
Esther's events fall in the reign of Xerxes (Ahasuerus), about 483-473 BC. This was after the temple was rebuilt in 516 BC and before Nehemiah's walls in 445 BC.
Ezekiel 38:5 names Persia and Cush. Esther 1:1 describes an empire 'from India to Cush'.

Other fulfilled or historical readers point to the Maccabean wars against Antiochus IV (167-164 BC). Some amillennialists see Gog as a symbol of the final world revolt at Christ's return. Futurists hold the battle is still ahead. Critics of the Esther view note that Esther never mentions Gog, and Esther 8:9 actually dates to Xerxes, not Darius.
What parallels link Esther and Ezekiel 38-39, and where do they differ?
Both describe enemies from across the Persian world planning to destroy and plunder a defenceless people, and God turning the attack back. Some details, such as plunder, differ.

On this reading, the parallels are strong. In both, the enemy plans to seize spoil (Ezekiel 38:12; Esther 3:13). In both, the attackers come from all over the empire, including Persia and Cush (Ezekiel 38:5; Esther 8:9). In both, God's people seem defenceless but win a complete reversal. In both, the nations then see God's hand. Ezekiel says the house of Israel will know the LORD from that day on (39:22). Esther says many from the peoples became Jews, because fear of the Jews had fallen on them (8:17). In both, the victory is remembered: by a valley named for Gog's army (Ezekiel 39:11) and by the feast of Purim (Esther 9:28). An honest note: Ezekiel says Israel will plunder its enemies (39:10). Esther stresses three times that the Jews did not take plunder (9:10, 15, 16).
Esther 8:17: many of the people of the land declared themselves Jews.
Esther 9:10, 15, 16: 'on the plunder they did not lay their hand.'
Ezekiel 39:11: the Valley of Hamon-gog (the multitude of Gog).

Critics of the view say the differences are too great. Esther has no birds feasting on the dead, no seven months of burial and no fire from heaven (Ezekiel 38:22). Ezekiel's language is cosmic: mountains overturned and the earth shaking. Futurists and many amillennialists say this points beyond any Persian-era event.
Why do prophecy teachers keep revising their books and their lists of end-time nations?
Because their identifications follow the news, not the text. When the Soviet Union fell, 'the nations of the north' moved to Muslim republics, and earlier books were quietly updated.

On this reading, frequent revision is a warning sign. When the Soviet Union broke up in 1991, Pat Robertson said he now thought the northern nations might be the Muslim republics, such as Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and Azerbaijan. That was a major change. It came from new headlines, not new study of Ezekiel. Many books have had new editions with new villains. John Walvoord's Armageddon, Oil and the Middle East Crisis (1974) was revised in 1990. Billy Graham's Approaching Hoofbeats (1983) became Storm Warning (1992). Few editions admit that the earlier version was wrong. God's word does not change with the news (Isaiah 40:8). If a prophecy reading must be rewritten every decade, the method may be faulty.
Walvoord's 'Armageddon, Oil and the Middle East Crisis' sold over a million copies in its 1990 revision during the Gulf crisis.
Thomas McCall and Zola Levitt, 'The Coming Russian Invasion of Israel' (1974), revised 1987 and 1992.
Isaiah 40:8: the word of our God stands forever.

Futurist authors reply that updates are honest attempts to watch events, not changes to Scripture. They say the core picture stays the same: a northern coalition, a revived Rome and a future Antichrist. Only the guesses about who fills each role change. Many also warn against sensational date-setting.
Is the European Union the revived Roman Empire with ten kings foretold in Daniel and Revelation?
On this reading, no. The 'ten kings' were fulfilled in the first century. The EU passed ten members long ago and does not match Rome's borders.

Many futurists teach that a ten-nation European union will become a revived Roman Empire ruled by Antichrist. They cite the ten toes (Daniel 2:41-42), the ten horns (Daniel 7:7, 24) and the ten kings (Revelation 17:12). The fulfilled reading answers in three ways. First, the theory needs a gap of two thousand years between Daniel's sixty-ninth and seventieth weeks, which Daniel does not mention. Second, Daniel never calls the toes kings. Third, the numbers have not fit. The European Community reached ten members in 1981 and twelve in 1986. The EU later grew to 28 and is now 27, after the UK left in 2020. Its borders still leave out much of the old empire: Syria, Egypt, North Africa and Judea.
Hal Lindsey (1970) taught that ten nations would come 'out of' Rome. The European Community had ten members in 1981.
Jacques Delors spoke in 1992 of a possible future EU of 35 members.
Earlier candidates for 'revived Rome' included Mussolini's empire, the League of Nations, the UN and NATO.

Futurists reply that the ten kings may be ten regions or leaders, not ten member states. They say the final empire need not match Rome's exact borders. Some note that the Western European Union had ten full members from 1995 to 2011. Amillennialists and historicists see the ten horns as the many kingdoms that followed Rome's fall.
Who were the 'ten kings' of Revelation 17:12 in the first century?
On this reading, the rulers of Rome's provinces and client kingdoms. They held power under the emperor and joined Rome's war against Jerusalem and the church.

Revelation 17:12 says the ten horns are ten kings who receive authority 'for one hour' with the beast. Their power is short and borrowed. On the fulfilled reading, these are the provincial rulers and client kings of Nero's day. Dean F. W. Farrar listed ten main imperial provinces: Italy, Achaia, Asia, Syria, Egypt, Africa, Spain, Gaul, Britain and Germany. Under Rome, local rulers were also called kings. Pilate and the crowd called Caesar 'king' (John 19:15). Herod Agrippa II was also 'King Agrippa' (Acts 25:13; 26:2). The commentator David S. Clark saw the ten horns as the kingdoms Rome had conquered. Some writers say there were never ten kings in the Roman Empire. History shows there were many local kings under Rome.
Acts 25:13: King Agrippa and Bernice came to greet Festus.
Client kings who sent troops to Titus in AD 70 included Agrippa II, Antiochus IV of Commagene, Sohaemus of Emesa and Malchus II of Nabataea (Tacitus, Histories 5.1; Josephus, Jewish War 3.4.2).
Revelation 17:12: they rule 'one hour' with the beast.

Futurists say these ten kings have 'not yet received a kingdom' (17:12) and fight the Lamb at his return (17:14). So they must be future. Historicists list ten barbarian kingdoms that rose from Rome's fall, such as the Franks and Vandals. Idealists see ten as a symbol of the full power of world rulers.
If the prophecies about Babylon, Rome and the ten kings are fulfilled, do they still speak to modern nations?
Yes. Fulfilled prophecy shows how God judges proud empires. Any nation that copies Babylon or Rome can expect the same kind of judgment.

The fourth key is to separate fulfilment from application. A prophecy may be fulfilled once, but the principle within it applies in every age. On this reading, the fall of Babylon and Rome gives a fixed point for judging current events. Political unions can be good or evil. Under Napoleon and Hitler, a united Europe was clearly evil, and both rulers fell. Later tyrants who acted like a Caesar or a Nebuchadnezzar met their own ruin. Psalm 2 warns kings to serve the LORD with fear and to honour the Son. Daniel says God's kingdom will crush rival kingdoms and stand forever (Daniel 2:44). Paul says Christ must reign until all enemies are under his feet (1 Corinthians 15:25). So Christians watch the news with hope, not panic.
Napoleon's empire fell in 1814-1815. Hitler's Reich, which promised a thousand years, lasted twelve (1933-1945).
Daniel 4:34-37: Nebuchadnezzar learned that the Most High rules the kingdoms of men.
Psalm 2:10-12: 'Be wise, O kings... kiss the Son.'

Christians of every view accept this principle of application. Futurists add that Revelation's Babylon and beast are also still future, so the warnings are both principle and prediction. Idealists say application is the main point, since the beast and Babylon appear in every age. Historicists see a continuing fulfilment through church history.
If these prophecies are past, what future hope do Christians still have?
A great hope. Christ reigns now and will put every enemy under his feet. His kingdom grows until the last enemy, death, is destroyed at his final coming.

On this reading, past fulfilment does not empty the future. It shows that God keeps his word on time. Christ is now seated at God's right hand (Acts 2:33-36). He received the kingdom promised in Daniel 7:13-14. That kingdom is like a stone that becomes a great mountain and fills the earth (Daniel 2:35). Rival kingdoms rise and fall, but his endures. Paul says Christ must reign until he has put all enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death (1 Corinthians 15:25-26). That will happen at the resurrection, when Christ appears (1 Corinthians 15:23, 52). The nations will finally worship him (Psalms 22:27; Philippians 2:10-11). So the believer works and prays with confidence, not fear.
Daniel 2:35: the stone became a great mountain and filled the whole earth.
Psalms 110:1, the Old Testament verse most quoted in the New Testament, promises enemies made a footstool.
Philippians 2:10-11: every knee will bow.

Futurists share this hope but place much of it after a future tribulation and a literal millennial reign from Jerusalem. Amillennialists see Christ reigning now with no great golden age before the end. Postmillennialists expect widespread gospel success first. Full preterists, unlike this partial view, place the resurrection in the past as well.
Does the time element play only a small part in Bible prophecy?
On the fulfilled reading, no. Time words are part of the message itself. A warning without a real time frame would lose its force.

One futurist textbook said the time element holds only a small place in prophecy. The fulfilled reading answers that timing is often the whole point. Jonah told Nineveh that the city would fall in forty days (Jonah 3:4). The people repented because the judgment was close. If they could have stretched forty days into four hundred years, the warning would have meant nothing. In the same way, Jesus told the crowds that the blood of the prophets would fall "upon this generation" (Matthew 23:36). The disciples asked "when" (Matthew 24:3), and Jesus gave a time frame (Matthew 24:34). Read this way, a prophecy's time words are as binding as its other words. If we ignore them, we change the prophecy.
Jonah 3:4-10: a forty-day warning moved a whole city to repent, and God held back the judgment.
Matthew 24:3 and 24:34: the disciples ask "when", and Jesus answers with "this generation".

Futurists reply that God's prophetic timetable can include long gaps the prophets did not see, as with Isaiah 61:1-2, where Jesus stopped reading mid-verse (Luke 4:19). They say the time words show certainty and urgency, not a date limit. Idealists say the words show that every age lives near the end.
Does any New Testament verse say Jesus could return "at any moment"?
The fulfilled reading says no verse uses that idea. The texts say the coming was "near" and "at hand" for the first readers, which is stronger than "could happen".
